lessons.title: The Funding Ladder: Bootstrapping, Friends and Family, Pre-Seed, Seed and Series A

children.text: Startup funding has its own vocabulary, and most of it is used loosely. One founder says "we closed our pre-seed", another says "we are raising a Series A", and both may have similar revenue. The labels are not legal categories. They are shorthand for how proven the business is, how much money changes hands and how much ownership goes with it. This lesson lays out the whole ladder in one view, then follows one company climbing it rung by rung.

body.text: Each rung of the funding ladder buys down a specific risk. Pre-seed money asks whether you can build it, seed money asks whether anyone wants it, and Series A money asks whether you can sell it again and again, profitably enough to be worth scaling.

children.text: The Whole Ladder in One Table

The cheque sizes below are typical Indian ranges seen in the mid-2020s, not rules. A deep tech hardware company may raise a ₹15 crore seed round, while a profitable services business may never raise anything at all.

body.text: Notice how the jumps get bigger. Going from seed to Series A is roughly a seven times bigger cheque, and investors expect the business to have changed just as much in between. This is the widest gap on the ladder, and Lesson 5.2 is devoted entirely to crossing it.

children.text: What Each Rung Really Means

markDefs.definition: Funding a company from the founders' own savings and the cash the business itself generates, without outside investors.

children.text: Bootstrapping

is the default, not the exception. Most Indian companies never raise a rupee of outside equity. A consulting firm, a manufacturing unit or a profitable software business can fund itself from customer payments. The trade is speed for control.
Friends and family

money arrives when there is nothing to show but conviction. It is the easiest money to get and the most expensive to lose, because failure is paid for in relationships, not just rupees. Treat it formally: proper paperwork, a clear share count and an honest warning that the money may never come back.
Pre-seed
is the first professional money. Angels and accelerators fund the build: a working prototype, the first few hundred users, the founding team. Nobody expects meaningful revenue yet.
Seed

money buys evidence. The product exists and some people pay for it. The round funds the search for repeatable demand: which customer, which channel, which price. Seed investors expect experiments, not predictability.
Series A

is a different conversation entirely. By now the experiments should be over. A Series A investor is not buying a hypothesis, they are buying a machine: spend ₹1 here, get ₹3 back there, reliably, and here is what happens when we feed ₹40 crore into it. That is why the round comes with a full term sheet, a board seat and real governance.

body.label: Why the letter matters more than the money
body.value: Series A is the first priced institutional round
body.context: Pre-seed and seed money often comes in through convertible instruments that postpone the valuation question. A Series A sets a formal price per share, a full term sheet and a board seat, which is why the label carries weight even when the amount does not.

body.title: Which rung is this company on?
body.question: A Hyderabad healthtech startup has a live app, 4,000 paying users, ₹40 lakh of annual revenue growing about 15% a month, and three months of data showing that customers from one channel pay back their acquisition cost in five months. It wants ₹8 crore to hire and expand to four more cities. Which round is this most likely to be?
body.explanation: Real paying customers and early evidence that acquisition works, but not yet a proven machine at scale. That is a classic seed profile, and ₹8 crore sits squarely in the Indian seed range. Series A investors would want many more months of consistent data and a far larger revenue base.

children.text: One Company, Three Rounds: FieldNote

FieldNote Technologies is an illustrative Nashik startup that helps grape and onion farmers plan harvests and find buyers. Follow it up the ladder and watch two numbers move in opposite directions: the money in the bank goes up, and the founders' ownership comes down.

events.title: Bootstrapped
events.description: Two co-founders quit their jobs, put in ₹12 lakh of savings and build a basic app used free by 60 farmers around Nashik. They own 100% of the company.

events.title: Friends and family: ₹30 lakh
events.description: An uncle and two former colleagues invest ₹30 lakh at a ₹3 crore post-money valuation, buying 10%. The money pays for a designer and eight months of runway.

events.title: Seed: ₹6 crore
events.description: With 3,000 farmers paying ₹500 a season and a mandi buyer signed up, a seed fund invests ₹6 crore at a ₹30 crore post-money valuation for 20%. A 10% ESOP pool is created as part of the round.

events.title: Series A: ₹24 crore
events.description: Revenue is ₹9 crore a year across three states, growing 12% a month, and each new district turns profitable within seven months. A VC fund invests ₹24 crore at a ₹120 crore post-money valuation for 20%, and takes a board seat.

body.caption: The rule behind every row of the table below. Lesson 3.1 unpacks it properly.

body.title: FieldNote ownership after the Series A (%)
Show me how those percentages were calculated

children.text: Every round issues new shares, so existing holders keep their share count and lose percentage. The shortcut is to multiply everyone's old percentage by the share of the company that is not newly issued.
Friends and family round:
investors take 10%, so the founders' 100% becomes 100% × 90% = 90%.
Seed round:
the seed fund takes 20% and a 10% ESOP pool is created, so 30% of the company is new. Existing holders keep 70% between them. Founders: 90% × 70% = 63%. Friends and family: 10% × 70% = 7%.
Series A:
the new fund takes 20%, so everyone else keeps 80% of what they had. Founders: 63% × 80% = 50.4%. Friends and family: 7% × 80% = 5.6%. Seed fund: 20% × 80% = 16%. ESOP pool: 10% × 80% = 8%.

One simplification: real Series A rounds usually top the ESOP pool back up to 10% or more, which dilutes the founders a little further. Lesson 3.4 shows how that negotiation works and who ends up paying for it.

body.title: What happened to the first cheque?
body.prompt: The friends and family investors put in ₹30 lakh for 10%. After the Series A they hold 5.6% of a company valued at ₹120 crore. What is their stake worth now, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 5.6% × ₹120 crore = ₹6.72 crore, about 22 times the ₹30 lakh they put in. Their percentage almost halved while their value multiplied, which is what healthy dilution looks like. Note the words "on paper": these shares cannot be sold on NSE tomorrow morning.

children.text: The Ladder Is Not Compulsory

Three corrections to the tidy picture above. First, plenty of startups skip rungs. A team with a strong track record can raise a large seed round straight away, and some go from bootstrapped to Series A. Second, most companies stop climbing. A seed round is not a promise of a Series A, and many good businesses raise once and then fund themselves. Third, some step off deliberately. "Seed strapping" describes a company that raises one round, reaches profitability and never raises again, keeping both ownership and control.

body.text: Never assume the next round follows automatically. Only a minority of seed-funded Indian startups ever raise a Series A, and the gap widens when funding markets turn cautious. Plan every round as though it is your last, which means turning it into either profitability or evidence strong enough to make the next round obvious.

body.title: Name the round
body.textWithBlank: The first priced institutional round, with a formal price per share, a full term sheet and usually a board seat, is the Series ___.
body.explanation: Earlier money often arrives through convertible instruments that postpone the valuation question. The Series A is where the company is formally priced and real governance begins.

body.title: Is this really a Series A?
body.scenario: Arjun runs a two-year-old Kochi logistics software startup. It raised ₹1.2 crore from angels 18 months ago. It now has 14 customers and ₹1.1 crore of annual recurring revenue, flat for the last two quarters, with about 9 months of runway left. Two customers contribute 60% of revenue. Arjun wants to raise ₹30 crore and is calling it a Series A because, in his words, "we already did our seed".
body.prompt: How will a VC fund read this, and what should Arjun do instead?
body.modelAnswer:
A VC will ignore the label and look at the evidence, which reads early seed, not Series A.
1. Flat revenue for two quarters is the killer. A Series A funds the scaling of a machine that already works. Nothing here is compounding.
2. Concentration risk: two customers are 60% of revenue. Losing one halves the business.
3. ₹30 crore against ₹1.1 crore of revenue is roughly 27 times revenue, very hard to justify without growth.
4. Nine months of runway means he is close to raising from weakness, exactly what Lesson 1.1 warned against.
Better plan: raise a smaller seed round of ₹4 crore to ₹6 crore, or a bridge from the existing angels, and spend it on one thing, restarting growth and adding customers so no single account is more than about 20% of revenue. Then raise a Series A on four to six quarters of consistent growth. Calling a round a Series A does not make investors treat it as one, and a failed Series A process leaves a trail that makes the next raise harder.

cards.definition: Funding the company from founders' savings and customer revenue, with no outside equity investors.
An early informal round, typically ₹5 lakh to ₹50 lakh, from people backing the founder rather than the numbers.
The first professional money, typically ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore, funding a prototype, founding team and first users.
Typically ₹2 crore to ₹15 crore, funding the search for repeatable demand once a product and early customers exist.
The first priced institutional round, typically ₹20 crore to ₹80 crore, funding the scaling of a proven growth engine.
Shares set aside for employee grants, usually created or topped up as part of a funding round.
Raising one early round, reaching profitability and then choosing never to raise again.

points: Round names describe how proven a business is, not a legal category. Investors read the evidence, never the label.
Each rung buys down one risk: can you build it, does anyone want it, and can you sell it repeatedly and profitably.
Typical Indian ranges: friends and family ₹5 lakh to ₹50 lakh, pre-seed ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore, seed ₹2 crore to ₹15 crore, Series A ₹20 crore to ₹80 crore.
Most rounds sell 15% to 25% of the company, so founders commonly fall from 100% to roughly half by the end of a Series A.
Dilution across rounds multiplies: each round leaves you with your old percentage times the share of the company not newly issued, as FieldNote's 100% to 50.4% shows.
A falling percentage can still mean a rising value. The ₹30 lakh friends and family cheque became 5.6% worth ₹6.72 crore on paper.
The ladder is optional. Startups skip rungs, stop climbing or step off deliberately, and only a minority of seed-funded companies ever raise a Series A.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Cheque sizes and stake ranges are typical market observations that shift with conditions, not standards. FieldNote Technologies, Arjun's company and the other examples are illustrative. Speak to a qualified professional before making funding decisions for your company.
